content: The updated Cochrane Review served as the evidence base for evaluating cervical priming methods for vacuum aspiration. This review included 61 studies, with 8 new studies added. Approximately half of these studies contributed to the development of the Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework. For surgical abortion at less than 12–14 weeks of gestation, misoprostol or mifepristone is suggested as cervical priming agents. Studies comparing misoprostol and mifepristone showed that the procedure time was shorter with misoprostol, but pre-procedure cervical dilation was greater with mifepristone. The side-effect profiles of both drugs were comparable, though evidence certainty was very low. For consistency, the gestational age cut-off for recommendations was set at 12 weeks, though evidence included pregnancies up to 14 weeks. High-certainty evidence supported a 3-hour interval between cervical priming and the procedure as optimal, though a 1-hour interval was also considered feasible based on expert panel discussions. For later gestational ages (≥12 weeks), cervical priming is recommended prior to surgical abortion. Between 12 and 19 weeks, medication alone (preferably mifepristone plus misoprostol) or a combination of medication and osmotic dilators is suggested. For gestations ≥19 weeks, a combination of osmotic dilators and medication is recommended. The interval between osmotic dilator placement and the procedure should not exceed two days. The expert panel highlighted the pharmacokinetic similarity of buccal and vaginal routes for misoprostol, with the sublingual route being more effective. The use of mifepristone with misoprostol is favored over misoprostol alone due to greater pre-procedure cervical dilation and shorter procedure times. Combining medication with laminaria is preferred over laminaria alone, as it results in higher cervical dilation, reduced need for further dilation, and shorter procedure times, particularly at higher gestational ages. Cervical priming beyond 12–14 weeks can be self-managed, saving travel time for women and staff time for osmotic dilator insertion. Community health workers (CHWs) and pharmacy workers have been recommended to provide medical abortion at <12 weeks, as this requires similar skills and knowledge. Pharmacists can dispense medications for cervical priming as part of the surgical abortion process, ensuring continuity of care. Evidence supports the safety and effectiveness of nurses and midwives providing manual vacuum aspiration, optimizing workflow and reducing waiting times for women. The expert panel emphasized that denial of cervical priming as part of abortion care may violate the right to non-discrimination and equality. Restrictions on which health workers can provide abortion care are inconsistent with WHO guidance and are not evidence-based. States must ensure adequate numbers of skilled providers and essential medicines to fulfill the right to health. WHO recommends against arbitrary regulations limiting who can provide abortion care, advocating for equitable access to quality services.
